lesson.title: Squaring Up the Triangle: Power Factor Correction
lesson.summary: Power factor correction adds capacitance in parallel with a lagging inductive load to cancel out unwanted reactive power, shrinking the current the source must supply without changing the real power the load actually uses. It is the standard fix wherever motors and transformers drag a power factor down and drive up utility bills.
lesson.body:
Most industrial loads, motors, transformers, fluorescent ballasts, are inductive, meaning their current lags their voltage and their power factor is less than 1 and described as lagging. A lagging power factor is a problem even though the load still gets all the real power (measured in watts) it needs, because the source and the wiring must also carry the reactive power (measured in VAR) that sloshes back and forth without doing any useful work, and that reactive current adds to the total current the utility's wires, transformers, and generators must be sized to handle. Power factor correction fixes this by adding a capacitor bank in parallel with the load. A capacitor draws a leading current, exactly out of step with the lagging current the inductive load draws, so the two reactive currents partially cancel, and the source only has to supply the leftover.

The calculation starts from the power triangle: real power P, reactive power Q, and apparent power S, related by S^2 = P^2 + Q^2, with power factor defined as cos(theta) = P/S. To correct a lagging power factor, you compute the reactive power the load demands, decide the reactive power you want left over after correction, and size a capacitor to supply exactly the difference, since a capacitor's reactive power is defined as negative (leading) relative to an inductor's positive (lagging) convention, so parallel capacitor VAR cancels load VAR directly.

Take a 10 kW load operating at 240 V rms, 60 Hz, with a lagging power factor of 0.6. The load angle is theta1 = arccos(0.6) = 53.13 degrees, and since cos and sin of that angle form a 3-4-5 triangle (0.6, 0.8, 1.0 scaled), tan(theta1) = 0.8/0.6 = 1.3333. The reactive power is Q1 = P x tan(theta1) = 10,000 W x 1.3333 = 13,333 VAR. Suppose the goal is to raise the power factor to 0.9 lagging. The new angle is theta2 = arccos(0.9) = 25.84 degrees, with sin(theta2) = sqrt(1 - 0.81) = sqrt(0.19) = 0.4359, so tan(theta2) = 0.4359/0.9 = 0.4843, giving Q2 = 10,000 x 0.4843 = 4,843 VAR.

The capacitor bank must cancel the difference: Qc = Q1 - Q2 = 13,333 - 4,843 = 8,490 VAR. Its reactance is found from Qc = V^2/Xc, so Xc = V^2/Qc = 240^2 / 8,490 = 57,600 / 8,490 = 6.78 ohms. Converting to capacitance at 60 Hz: C = 1/(2*pi*f*Xc) = 1/(2*pi x 60 x 6.78) = 1/2,557.7 = 3.91 x 10^-4 F, or about 391 microfarads. That single parallel capacitor bank cuts the reactive burden nearly in half and reduces the total current the source must supply, all without touching the 10 kW of real power the load actually consumes, which is the entire point of power factor correction.

The result is worth stating in terms of current, since that is what utilities and wiring actually feel. Before correction, apparent power was S1 = P/pf1 = 10,000/0.6 = 16,667 VA, meaning the source current was I1 = 16,667/240 = 69.4 A rms. After correction to 0.9, apparent power drops to S2 = 10,000/0.9 = 11,111 VA, so the source current falls to I2 = 11,111/240 = 46.3 A rms. That is a 33 percent cut in current for the exact same 10 kW of delivered work, which is why utilities frequently offer rate incentives, or levy penalties, tied directly to a customer's power factor: correcting it with capacitors like the leading-power-factor bank sized here shrinks generation and wiring costs without asking the customer to use one less watt.
